description: The fiery backbone of Andhra gastronomy. Slender, deep crimson chillies with high capsaicin content and high natural red coloring agent (ASTA color value 80-100). Imparts unmistakable biting heat and vibrant ruby hue to karams, pickles, and curries.
traditionalProcessing: Sun-dried on clean riverbank terraces, destemmed by hand, and pounded in granite mortars with sea salt.

geographicalIndication: Indigenous to Guntur, Krishna, and Godavari deltas
description: Known as the Andhra Shakambhari (patron culinary plant). The red-stemmed variety (Erra Gongura) contains potent oxalic and malic acid that provides an assertive sour, earthy flavor that cuts through heavy meats and rich dals.
traditionalProcessing: Plucked fresh, washed thoroughly, dry-wilted in unrefined sesame oil without water, and pounded in stone mortars.

geographicalIndication: Rayalaseema Dryland Plateau (Anantapur, Kurnool, Kadapa, Chittoor)
description: Ancient drought-tolerant super-grain packed with calcium, dietary fiber, and complex carbohydrates. Sustained agrarian communities across the Rayalaseema plateau for millennia.
traditionalProcessing: Sun-dried whole grains, coarsely stone-milled in stone chakki (tirugali) without removing the outer husk.

description: Matured sour pods stored in ceramic bharanis with sea salt until the color deepens from amber to dark mahogany-black. Develops a complex, mellow, wine-like acidity without raw astringency.
traditionalProcessing: Deseeded by hand, salted, kneaded into tight balls, and aged in darkness for 1 to 3 years.

geographicalIndication: Ongole, Krishna, and Godavari dairy belts
description: Golden clarified butter prepared by boiling whole raw milk, fermenting into curd with ancestral cultures, churning into butter with a wooden bilona (kavvam), and slow-clarifying over cow-dung embers with betel or drumstick leaves.
culinaryUses: Topping on Ragi Sangati & Mudda Pappu
traditionalProcessing: Traditional Bilona method preserving butyric acid, nutty aroma, and golden granulations.

geographicalIndication: Anantapuramu District — largest groundnut belt in Andhra Pradesh
description: The agrarian lifeline of Rayalaseema. Raw, unpolished groundnuts slow-roasted in sand-filled iron kadais until the papery skins crack and release deep toasted aromas. Used as both a base for gravies and cold-pressed into the primary cooking oil of southern Andhra.
culinaryUses: Cold-pressed groundnut oil for deep frying
traditionalProcessing: Dried in the pod under sun, hand-shelled, and slow-roasted in hot sand in a concave iron wok.

description: Tiny ivory seeds with immense nutritional density and a rich, toasty flavor when dry-roasted. Essential in Andhra spice pastes for curry stuffings and chutneys. Cold-pressed into nuvvula noone (sesame oil), the traditional cooking fat of coastal Andhra.
traditionalProcessing: Dry-roasted on low heat until seeds pop and turn pale gold, then stone-ground with spices.

description: Small, olive-green whole lentils (moong) with intact skin, prized for their fresh, grassy aroma and high plant protein. Soaked and wet-ground into smooth batter without fermentation to make Pesarattu and pesara pappu.
traditionalProcessing: Soaked whole in cold water for 4-6 hours, then wet-ground on rolu (stone grinder) with minimal water.

geographicalIndication: Godavari and Krishna delta paddy fields
description: Medium-grain aromatic paddy variety acclaimed for its light, fluffy texture, low glycemic starch, and subtle jasmine-like fragrance. The daily staple grain of Andhra meals, served steaming hot with ghee, pappu, and pulusu.
culinaryUses: Daily steamed rice with pappu and ghee
traditionalProcessing: Hand-harvested, sun-dried on granite threshing floors, and parboiled or polished in village hullers.

geographicalIndication: Anakapalli (Asia's 2nd largest jaggery market), Srikakulam, and Vizianagaram
description: Unrefined, golden-to-dark-brown blocks of concentrated sugarcane juice, boiled in massive brass vessels until thick and crystallized. Retains minerals, iron, and deep molasses-toffee flavor absent in refined white sugar.
traditionalProcessing: Fresh cane juice clarified with lime, boiled in open brass pans (gannela aadam), poured into wooden molds, and sun-solidified.

geographicalIndication: Vizianagaram, Srikakulam, and northern coastal Andhra
description: Tiny jet-black spheres that crackle and pop in hot oil, releasing a sharp, nutty pungency fundamental to every Andhra talimpu (tempering). Also ground into aavapindi (mustard powder) for Uttarandhra pickles and stews.
culinaryUses: Talimpu (tempering) base for every dal and curry
traditionalProcessing: Sun-dried whole seeds, stored in clay pots. For aavapindi, dry-roasted lightly and stone-ground into coarse pungent powder.

geographicalIndication: Ubiquitous across all 26 districts of Andhra Pradesh
description: Glossy, dark-green, deeply aromatic leaves from the Murraya koenigii tree. Releases an intensely fragrant, slightly citrusy, peppery oil when spluttered in hot oil or ghee. No Andhra dish is complete without karivepaku in its talimpu.
culinaryUses: Essential talimpu aromatic in every curry
Fresh garnish on rasam and charu
Fried crisp in ghee for biryani
traditionalProcessing: Plucked fresh from backyard trees, washed, and added whole sprigs directly into spluttering hot oil. Never dried.

geographicalIndication: Kadapa, Kurnool, and Duggirala (Krishna) — major Andhra turmeric belts
description: Bright orange-gold rhizome of Curcuma longa, essential for its antiseptic properties, golden color, and earthy-bitter warmth. Added in measured pinches to nearly every Andhra preparation as both a flavoring and a preservative.
culinaryUses: Universal base spice in curries, dals, pulusus
traditionalProcessing: Boiled whole in copper vessels, sun-dried for 15 days, and stone-ground into fine golden powder.

description: Small, hard, amber-brown seeds with an intensely bitter yet aromatic maple-like flavor. Dry-roasted and ground into menthi podi, they add depth and a distinctive umami-bitter backbone to pulusus, pickles, and chutneys.
culinaryUses: Menthi Podi (fenugreek spice powder) for Chepala Pulusu
traditionalProcessing: Dry-roasted on iron tawa until dark amber and fragrant, then coarsely stone-ground. Over-roasting turns them acrid.

geographicalIndication: Konaseema and East Godavari coconut groves
description: The tall coconut palms of the Godavari delta provide both fresh white kernel (for chutneys, sweets, and gravies) and copra (dried coconut, grated into stuffing masalas). Coconut oil and milk are fundamental to Konaseema cuisine.
traditionalProcessing: Fresh kernel grated on a rotating iron scraper (thuranam). For dry coconut, copra is sun-dried for 2 weeks and grated fine.
